steps.title: Change a command with a dot

say.never: Every command has helper methods you can add on the end with a dot. They don't change the original: they wrap it in a new command that behaves a little differently, mostly by changing **when it finishes** or **what runs with it**. They are called **decorators**.
say.bit: Add a helper on the end with a dot to wrap a command in a new one. Decorators change when it finishes or what runs with it.

say.never: `.withTimeout(2.0)` stops the command after two seconds if it hasn't finished already. A command that never finishes on its own, like `shoot()`, now has an end: the timeout is the condition. When it times out, the wrapped command's `end(true)` runs, so it still cleans up.
say.bit: `withTimeout(seconds)` stops a command after that long. It still cleans up through `end`.

say.never: `.until(condition)` finishes the command as soon as your yes/no condition becomes true, or whenever the command itself finishes, whichever comes first. It is a custom `isFinished` without writing a class.
say.bit: `until(condition)` finishes the command as soon as your yes/no condition is true.

marks.label: the condition: a ball just left

say.never: `first.andThen(second)` runs `first` until it finishes, then runs `second`. This is the same as `Commands.sequence(first, second)`, written as a chain. Pick it when two steps read naturally as "this, then that".
say.bit: `a.andThen(b)` runs a until it finishes, then b. Same as a sequence of two.

say.never: `a.alongWith(b)` starts both together and finishes when **both** are done. Pick it when two things can happen at once, like driving while the shooter spins up. If you'd rather stop when the first one finishes, `raceWith` does that.
say.bit: `a.alongWith(b)` runs both together and finishes when both are done.

marks.label: so this side can finish too

say.never: Read a chain left to right, one decorator at a time, and ask each time: when does this stop? Here the shot ends after two seconds (`withTimeout`), and the drive only starts once the turn has finished (`andThen`). Each dot builds a new, bigger command, and `Commands.sequence` from the next guide does the same for longer lists.
say.bit: Read a chain left to right and ask of each dot: when does this stop?
